items.title: I worked 13-hour days building my startup while working at Apple. Here's why I ignored advice to go all in sooner.
items.summary: Julie Zhu built her startup before and after work while she was still employed at Apple. Julie Zhu Julie Zhu spent eight months building her startup while working full time at Apple. She structured her days around both jobs, often working about 13 hours. She waited to quit until she felt financially secure and confident in her business. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Julie Zhu, a 29-year-old entrepreneur in New York City who left Apple last year to focus on her startup, Odd One In. The following has been edited for length and clarity. A few years ago, I started considering leaving my job at Apple and making the leap into entrepreneurship. A lot of people around me thought the decision was obvious: I should just quit. There were a few factors nudging me out the door. For one, I had wanted to become a founder since I was 18. I'd also developed a sort of love-hate relationship with Apple, where I began working in 2022. I was grateful for what I learned there, but I felt like it was a high-pressure, high-stress environment — and I also struggled with imposter syndrome. I wanted to build something where I had more of a say and could make more decisions. When I sought advice from people I knew, including those in the startup community, about 95% told me, "Julie, if you're not happy at Apple, you should just quit." They said I had the perfect résumé and that venture capital firms would likely be willing to give me money — or at least talk to me. They thought it was fine that I hadn't fully figured out my business idea yet. I realized I didn't have to follow the path that worked for other people. I wanted to chart my own. Quitting before I felt prepared wasn't the right decision for me. Business Insider is speaking with workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations. Share your story by filling out this form . I wanted a plan before I quit I think a lot of people who told me to quit gave me that advice because they'd found success in the startup world , which made it easier for them to tell me to take the risk. The truth is no one knows what it's like to walk in your shoes — or what decision is right for you. For me, completing a checklist I'd given myself before leaving Apple was really important. That included having a tangible idea I believed in, a team, and enough of a foundation to feel like I wasn't jumping completely blind. Financial security mattered a lot. I wanted to make sure I had about three to five years of runway across my assets and savings, including my Apple stock. I also wanted my family's support. My parents are entrepreneurs, and I wanted them to understand why I was giving up a comfortable corporate job, particularly when layoffs were happening across the tech industry. As I reflected on the best course of action, I talked everything through with my therapist. I wanted to be rational and logical about my decision. Julie Zhu waited to leave Apple until she felt confident about her startup's trajectory and her financial security. Julie Zhu My business idea started coming together By late 2024, some of those pieces were starting to come together. I found a cofounder who was already a friend of mine. Having that existing friendship and trust made it much easier for us to start building something together. From there, we started developing an idea I'd had for Odd One In, an artist collectible company. We officially started the business in December 2024, but I wasn't ready to leave Apple. So I decided to do both. Before incorporating Odd One In, I checked with Apple's business conduct team to make sure I could work on my company while employed there, and started building it outside my Apple work hours. For the next eight months, that meant structuring nearly my entire day around my two jobs. I built my startup before and after work While building my startup and working full-time at Apple, I would wake up around 5:30 a.m. and go to the gym — usually doing some cardio to wake myself up and stay healthy. Then I'd work on Odd One In from around 6 to 8 a.m. After that, I'd head to Apple for my day job. I'd typically get home around 5 p.m., eat, and start working on the startup again. I'd often work until around 10:30 p.m., then go to sleep and do it all over again the next day. On a typical weekday, I was spending roughly 13 to 14 hours working across Apple and the startup. It was a demanding schedule, but I had a plan for my business with specific milestones I wanted to achieve. That made the extra work feel intentional, rather than like I was just "working all the time." I finally felt ready to go all in and quit my job By August 2025, juggling both my Apple job and Odd One In had become too much, in part because my business was demanding more of my time. I also didn't think continuing was fair to my team at Apple . I'd found something I was more passionate about, and many of the pieces I'd wanted in place before quitting had come together. This included getting my parents' support for my decision to leave Apple. It took time for them to understand why the move was important to me, but once they understood my reasoning and saw real traction from what we were building, they became much more supportive. Overall, I finally felt confident that after four years with the company, it was the right time to move on. I'm glad I didn't quit before I was comfortable Since leaving, being a founder has been humbling, but it's also given me confidence. At Apple, I sometimes felt like a small part of a huge company. Building something from zero to one has shown me I'm capable of doing much more. Odd One In generated close to six figures in annual revenue last year, but I'm not paying myself a salary yet because we're reinvesting the money to grow the business, including production, warehousing, paying artists, and other expenses. We're completely bootstrapped: We haven't raised any outside funding and launched with our own savings. To pay my personal expenses, I've relied on the savings I accumulated while working at Apple and earlier in my career. Looking back, I'm glad I didn't follow the advice to quit before I was comfortable. There's a romanticized idea in the startup world that you have to take the leap and figure everything out afterward. That can work for some people. For me, spending eight months doing both made me feel confident in my decision to go all in. Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at jzinkula@businessinsider.com , or via Signal at jzinkula.29. Read the original article on Business Insider

I was grateful for what I learned there, but I felt like it was a high-pressure, high-stress environment — and I also struggled with imposter syndrome. I wanted to build something where I had more of a say and could make more decisions.

When I sought advice from people I knew, including those in the startup community, about 95% told me, "Julie, if you're not happy at Apple, you should just quit."

They said I had the perfect résumé and that venture capital firms would likely be willing to give me money — or at least talk to me. They thought it was fine that I hadn't fully figured out my business idea yet.

I realized I didn't have to follow the path that worked for other people. I wanted to chart my own. Quitting before I felt prepared wasn't the right decision for me.

Business Insider is speaking with workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations.

Share your story by filling out this form.

I wanted a plan before I quit

I think a lot of people who told me to quit gave me that advice because they'd found success in the startup world, which made it easier for them to tell me to take the risk.

The truth is no one knows what it's like to walk in your shoes — or what decision is right for you.

For me, completing a checklist I'd given myself before leaving Apple was really important. That included having a tangible idea I believed in, a team, and enough of a foundation to feel like I wasn't jumping completely blind.

Financial security mattered a lot. I wanted to make sure I had about three to five years of runway across my assets and savings, including my Apple stock.

I also wanted my family's support. My parents are entrepreneurs, and I wanted them to understand why I was giving up a comfortable corporate job, particularly when layoffs were happening across the tech industry.

As I reflected on the best course of action, I talked everything through with my therapist. I wanted to be rational and logical about my decision.

Julie Zhu waited to leave Apple until she felt confident about her startup's trajectory and her financial security.

Julie Zhu

My business idea started coming together

By late 2024, some of those pieces were starting to come together. I found a cofounder who was already a friend of mine. Having that existing friendship and trust made it much easier for us to start building something together.

From there, we started developing an idea I'd had for Odd One In, an artist collectible company. We officially started the business in December 2024, but I wasn't ready to leave Apple. So I decided to do both.

Before incorporating Odd One In, I checked with Apple's business conduct team to make sure I could work on my company while employed there, and started building it outside my Apple work hours.

For the next eight months, that meant structuring nearly my entire day around my two jobs.

I built my startup before and after work

While building my startup and working full-time at Apple, I would wake up around 5:30 a.m. and go to the gym — usually doing some cardio to wake myself up and stay healthy. Then I'd work on Odd One In from around 6 to 8 a.m.

After that, I'd head to Apple for my day job. I'd typically get home around 5 p.m., eat, and start working on the startup again. I'd often work until around 10:30 p.m., then go to sleep and do it all over again the next day. On a typical weekday, I was spending roughly 13 to 14 hours working across Apple and the startup.

It was a demanding schedule, but I had a plan for my business with specific milestones I wanted to achieve. That made the extra work feel intentional, rather than like I was just "working all the time."

I finally felt ready to go all in and quit my job

By August 2025, juggling both my Apple job and Odd One In had become too much, in part because my business was demanding more of my time.

I also didn't think continuing was fair to my team at Apple. I'd found something I was more passionate about, and many of the pieces I'd wanted in place before quitting had come together.

This included getting my parents' support for my decision to leave Apple. It took time for them to understand why the move was important to me, but once they understood my reasoning and saw real traction from what we were building, they became much more supportive.

Overall, I finally felt confident that after four years with the company, it was the right time to move on.

I'm glad I didn't quit before I was comfortable

Since leaving, being a founder has been humbling, but it's also given me confidence. At Apple, I sometimes felt like a small part of a huge company. Building something from zero to one has shown me I'm capable of doing much more.

Odd One In generated close to six figures in annual revenue last year, but I'm not paying myself a salary yet because we're reinvesting the money to grow the business, including production, warehousing, paying artists, and other expenses. We're completely bootstrapped: We haven't raised any outside funding and launched with our own savings. To pay my personal expenses, I've relied on the savings I accumulated while working at Apple and earlier in my career.

Looking back, I'm glad I didn't follow the advice to quit before I was comfortable. There's a romanticized idea in the startup world that you have to take the leap and figure everything out afterward. That can work for some people.

For me, spending eight months doing both made me feel confident in my decision to go all in.

items.title: I'm the CEO of Oura. I wake up at 5 a.m. when things are going well, and 3:30 a.m. when they're not. Here's what a day in my life looks like.
items.summary: Jason Henry for BI This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tom Hale, the 57-year-old CEO of Oura Health , based in San Francisco. It's been edited for length and clarity. I became the CEO of Oura in March 2022. We make the Oura Ring , a smart ring that delivers personalized health data and insights to help people live more balanced lives. My career spans more than 30 years in technology and consumer products, including serving as president of SurveyMonkey . Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. Here's what a typical day in my life in San Francisco looks like. 5 a.m. — No alarm necessary I wake up around 5 a.m. every day without an alarm. The first thing I do is check my Oura Ring. I want to know how I slept and how I'm set up for the day. I have a little competition going with my wife and kids over our scores. Based on what the data tells me, I start making small decisions about how to approach the day. If my score is lower than normal, I take it easy and defer major decisions. If my score is higher than normal, I'll push myself in workouts and at work. Jason Henry for BI When the business is going well, I sleep until 5 a.m. When it's not, I wake up at 3:30 a.m. and try to get back to sleep. 5:30 a.m. — The two minutes I try to protect I shower, and for the last two minutes, I do a breathing exercise . I'm not a meditation person, but my breathing exercise helps me get centered before I start my day. Sadly, it's the first thing that drops off when I'm pressed for time or dealing with a crisis. 6 a.m. — Information overload By 6 a.m., I'm showered, shaved, and ready to start the day. The data I receive first thing in the morning from the company stats, news, and overnight events from Finland, where a good portion of our company is based, affects how my day goes, whether it's bad news, good news, or both. I check my email and take my supplements. I do intermittent fasting , so my first meal of the day is around lunchtime. I then look at three critical sources of information: our daily sales data, listings of our products on eBay, and news digests. Jason Henry for BI For news, I rely on curators who compile information. I always read The Information's daily newsletter by Jessica Lessin and Headlines by Abe Burns. LinkedIn is where I'm most active. It has great content, but it sucks me down rabbit holes, so I use a timer app that limits my social media time. 6:30 a.m. — Walking to work I walk to work every day. It takes me half an hour, and I end up climbing a couple of pretty steep hills. During the walk, I'll listen to podcasts or take calls from my team. Jason Henry for BI When I'm traveling, I try to get a run in or take a walk around the city. I travel to Finland three or four times a year, plus regular trips to the UK, Europe, and Washington, DC. 8 a.m. — The early morning anxiety I'm most anxious and stressed in the early morning. Getting into the swing of things calms me down. The first thing I do when I get to the office is make a list in one of my accounting notebooks. Every time I cross something off, I feel like I'm making progress against whatever the challenge of the day is. You'll probably laugh at this, but in our all-hands meetings, we have a section called "Keeping Me Up at Night" and "Helping Me Sleep Soundly." That's how I communicate to the team what I'm worried about and what's going great. It helps them understand what to pay attention to. 9 a.m. — Standing desk, open floor plan, no trophies My workspace is pretty Spartan, no work trophies or memorabilia. I work at a standing desk. Our office has an open floor plan. Anyone can stop by with an idea or a question. Jason Henry for BI I've developed a weekly cadence. On Mondays, my direct reports have their staff meetings, but I check in. Tuesdays are my staff meetings, structured with clear agendas. On Wednesdays, I work through my to-do list with a mix of ad hoc meetings. Thursdays are for customers and partners. Fridays are for deep work. Noon — Two meals on repeat I eat my first meal at my desk around noon. I usually order a meal from Proper Food and rotate between two orders: a salad with chicken or salmon on rice with teriyaki sauce. After lunch and during the day, I take five-minute breaks to walk around the office. We have an outdoor deck and a bocce ball court where you can get some steps in. Jason Henry for BI 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. — My most productive period I get a lot done between 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. I send proactive emails, flag what we need to focus on, and schedule the rest for when I get enough information to make a decision. I usually leave the office between 6:30 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. and walk home. There are moments when it all feels overwhelming From age 30, when I had my first kid, to my early 50s, I was sleep-deprived and stressed pretty much all the time. I drank more coffee and ground through it. I wore an Oura Ring before I ever joined the company, so I came into this job already believing in the data. These days, I don't drink caffeine anymore, I get more sleep, and I'm very intentional about how I attack problems. Jason Henry for BI This job is harder and more demanding than anything I've ever done, but it's also the one where I feel best equipped to manage it. Evening routine — Physical books and bed by 9 p.m. I eat dinner with my wife. We share the cooking, and our go-to meals are salad with chicken or spaghetti squash with lamb meatballs in tomato sauce. Then we'll watch TV or read together. Right now, I'm reading "King of Kings," which is about the fall of the Shah of Iran, and "How the Body Knows Its Mind," which is about the interaction of mental and physical health. My wife and I go to bed around 8:30 p.m. or 9 p.m. I put on a sleep mask and earplugs, keep the room dark, and take magnesium and melatonin before bed. I use an Eight Sleep bed cooler . I set it at -3°C below ambient temperature. I've found that consistency in going to bed at the same time daily matters more than the duration of sleep. Jason Henry for BI Weekends — Walks, poodles, and backgammon On weekends, I like to go for walks with friends. I also go for runs with my dogs. I have two large poodles. They're a handful. The most important thing I do on the weekends is spend time with my family. Sometimes we do separate activities in the same room, or we play backgammon together. I also play guitar, but that's when I want to enjoy some alone time. Using the sauna has been a massive unlock for me. I aim for once or twice a week, and if I'm at the gym, I always end my workout with a session. In San Francisco, there's a spot right on the water where you can rotate between the heat and a jump in the cold bay. That contrast therapy is incredibly energizing. items.title: How decoding beluga whales’ chitchat may save them – and teach us more about ourselves
items.summary: From humpbacks learning the latest songs to sperm whales’ ‘clan codas’, drones and AI learning are helping reveal another dimension to the concept of culture In 2015, the whale researcher Valeria Vergara pitched a small tent at the icy water’s edge on Somerset Island in the remote Canadian high Arctic, shrouded in a freezing fog so thick she struggled to see her own hands. She trailed a cord out to the coast and plopped a hydrophone into the water to record the calls of belugas. As many as 1,000 of the whales, accompanied by their newborn calves, frequented the surrounding bay. Belugas’ ceaseless chatter, made up of dozens of unique sounds, is crucial to keeping these creatures connected in the dim, turbid waters of the Arctic. Continue reading...

items.title: Everyone hates performative LinkedIn posts. Workers feel like they have to write them anyway.
items.summary: Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI Many workers feel they need to build a personal brand on LinkedIn to get ahead. Some companies are even paying ghostwriters to create LinkedIn posts for their employees. The posting arms race has also fueled performative content, oversharing, and AI slop. Workers on LinkedIn are finding themselves in a catch-22: They may cringe at the self-promotional, carefully polished posts that fill their feeds, but still believe they need to build a personal brand of their own. Some companies are even stepping in to post for them. Corporate ghostwriting firm Hat Tip creates LinkedIn posts for founders and, increasingly, their employees. Founder Christian Di Bratto calls it a sales and marketing strategy for a world where brands may be losing their appeal. He recently quoted a client $8,400 a month to write LinkedIn posts for three employees, three times a week. "People want to buy from people," Di Bratto said. "This employee portion of it is the next evolution of what founder-led content was. With the rise of grindslop and the migration away from X, LinkedIn is now a hybrid of performative professional posting and personal sharing. Many workers view posting there as a necessary career investment , made easier by the rise of AI tools. Even LinkedIn is rethinking all this posting. In July, the company started letting users flag posts that seem "like AI slop." Pangram, an AI-detection firm, estimated that 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts and 30% of shorter posts it analyzed between April and June were likely AI-generated . LinkedIn says its recent changes have reduced the amount of AI slop on the platform. Why workers feel like they need to post so much on LinkedIn When a former Microsoft manager was laid off last year, he began regularly posting on LinkedIn about his field. After seeing recruiters and career coaches online emphasize the importance of building a personal brand on the platform, it felt like something he couldn't afford not to try. "We all have to be content creators on top of our actual jobs — or lack of jobs — and perform being a candidate," he said. It's not just struggling job seekers who've come to view regular LinkedIn posting as a key part of managing their careers. Muskan Agarwal, who is based in India and runs Cherry Media, a marketing agency that helps professionals and creators grow their online presence, said she's seen a surge in tech workers looking to build personal brands on platforms like LinkedIn. Her clients include current and former US-based employees of companies including Microsoft, Amazon, and Google. Agarwal said some aren't trying to become full-time creators, and that their goals include landing better jobs, speaking opportunities, or professional connections. Each client, she said, pays her agency for at least three months of services. Do you have a story to share about posting on LinkedIn? Reach out to these reporters at jzinkula@businessinsider.com and jkaplan@businessinsider.com . Does posting on LinkedIn actually help your career? The million-dollar question for job seekers and workers alike is how much all that posting actually helps their careers. Matt Stabile, founder of the recruiting firm Stabile Search, believes LinkedIn posts have shifted toward engagement-driven content. "The quality has skewed towards 'AI slop' rather than meaningful discussions," he said. Stabile believes posting and attracting engagement can increase someone's visibility on LinkedIn and help establish them as a thought leader, but that posting too much could send the wrong signal to recruiters. "I would say that overposting would be a red flag. If you are busy, in demand and talented, why would you spend your time posting on LinkedIn?" Jason Baxter, the owner and operator of a boutique marketing agency, posts one to two times a week and comments on posts at least ten times a week. He's gotten legitimate business and connections from the platform. Even so, he thinks that over half of the people on LinkedIn are just "out there shouting at the world and not reading what anyone else is saying." How to post without overdoing it Jansel Murad, a vice president at Dukas Linden Public Relations, a financial PR firm, generally recommends clients share one to two posts a week. "If you don't have something authentic to say, hold back, it's okay," Murad said. "Because then you'll probably get further engagement from your network when they see you really sharing updates that matter to you." And even if your authentic voice — which Murad said often seems to hit a sweet spot for the LinkedIn algorithm — wants to be out there five times a week, she would still say to hold back on that rapidity of posting. Instead, maybe bundle posts together. Ultimately, then, the best practice might just be a balance — and, sometimes, leaning into the cringe. Benjamin Chipman, a 25-year-old marketer and content creator who loves posting on LinkedIn, bristles at the concept of a performative poster. Chipman found posting on the platform life-changing during college, and says LinkedIn has been responsible for the majority of his career trajectory. "I don't care if you're posting on Instagram, on LinkedIn, on Facebook, there's a performance element to it all, but it doesn't mean it's inherently not productive," Chipman said. "Those two things can be true at the same time." Read the original article on Business Insider

With the rise of grindslop and the migration away from X, LinkedIn is now a hybrid of performative professional posting and personal sharing. Many workers view posting there as a necessary career investment, made easier by the rise of AI tools.

Even LinkedIn is rethinking all this posting. In July, the company started letting users flag posts that seem "like AI slop." Pangram, an AI-detection firm, estimated that 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts and 30% of shorter posts it analyzed between April and June were likely AI-generated. LinkedIn says its recent changes have reduced the amount of AI slop on the platform.

Why workers feel like they need to post so much on LinkedIn

When a former Microsoft manager was laid off last year, he began regularly posting on LinkedIn about his field. After seeing recruiters and career coaches online emphasize the importance of building a personal brand on the platform, it felt like something he couldn't afford not to try.

"We all have to be content creators on top of our actual jobs — or lack of jobs — and perform being a candidate," he said.

It's not just struggling job seekers who've come to view regular LinkedIn posting as a key part of managing their careers.

Muskan Agarwal, who is based in India and runs Cherry Media, a marketing agency that helps professionals and creators grow their online presence, said she's seen a surge in tech workers looking to build personal brands on platforms like LinkedIn.

Her clients include current and former US-based employees of companies including Microsoft, Amazon, and Google. Agarwal said some aren't trying to become full-time creators, and that their goals include landing better jobs, speaking opportunities, or professional connections. Each client, she said, pays her agency for at least three months of services.

Do you have a story to share about posting on LinkedIn? Reach out to these reporters at jzinkula@businessinsider.com and jkaplan@businessinsider.com.

Does posting on LinkedIn actually help your career?

The million-dollar question for job seekers and workers alike is how much all that posting actually helps their careers. Matt Stabile, founder of the recruiting firm Stabile Search, believes LinkedIn posts have shifted toward engagement-driven content.

"The quality has skewed towards 'AI slop' rather than meaningful discussions," he said.

Stabile believes posting and attracting engagement can increase someone's visibility on LinkedIn and help establish them as a thought leader, but that posting too much could send the wrong signal to recruiters.

"I would say that overposting would be a red flag. If you are busy, in demand and talented, why would you spend your time posting on LinkedIn?"

Jason Baxter, the owner and operator of a boutique marketing agency, posts one to two times a week and comments on posts at least ten times a week. He's gotten legitimate business and connections from the platform. Even so, he thinks that over half of the people on LinkedIn are just "out there shouting at the world and not reading what anyone else is saying."

How to post without overdoing it

Jansel Murad, a vice president at Dukas Linden Public Relations, a financial PR firm, generally recommends clients share one to two posts a week.

"If you don't have something authentic to say, hold back, it's okay," Murad said. "Because then you'll probably get further engagement from your network when they see you really sharing updates that matter to you."

And even if your authentic voice — which Murad said often seems to hit a sweet spot for the LinkedIn algorithm — wants to be out there five times a week, she would still say to hold back on that rapidity of posting. Instead, maybe bundle posts together.

Ultimately, then, the best practice might just be a balance — and, sometimes, leaning into the cringe.

Benjamin Chipman, a 25-year-old marketer and content creator who loves posting on LinkedIn, bristles at the concept of a performative poster. Chipman found posting on the platform life-changing during college, and says LinkedIn has been responsible for the majority of his career trajectory.

"I don't care if you're posting on Instagram, on LinkedIn, on Facebook, there's a performance element to it all, but it doesn't mean it's inherently not productive," Chipman said. "Those two things can be true at the same time."

items.title: The chips powering AI can take years to design. This startup says AI did it in 2 weeks.
items.summary: Architect Labs cofounders Ebrahim Hussain and Aaditya Subedi. Bonnie Rae Mills The startup Architect Labs says it used AI to design and verify a chip in two weeks. An AI model running on the chip then found ways to improve it, its 20-year-old cofounder said. Researchers called the speed impressive, though they said manufacturing will be the ultimate test. AI is coming for one of the hardest jobs in the technology industry: chip design . The nascent startup Architect Labs, founded last year, is betting on the promise of using AI to accelerate design for both chipmakers and companies seeking custom hardware. It says it designed and verified a chip called Redwood in two weeks, with two human chip architects setting and refining the overall plan while AI handled the detailed design work. It would dramatically speed up a process that typically takes a year or more, costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and requires large, specialized teams of around 100 people, the company said. This lengthy timeline is especially problematic in AI, where models evolve faster than the chips they run on, said Architect Labs cofounder and CEO Ebrahim Hussain, who is 20. Architect emerged from stealth in June with a $24 million seed round led by Kindred Ventures. Google's former chief scientist, Jeff Dean, and other executives from OpenAI and Nvidia also backed the startup. Hao Zheng, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Central Florida, called the Redwood timeline "impressive," though he said several startups and more established companies, such as Synopsys, also use AI to accelerate the chip design process. The Redwood experiment revealed something else, said Hussain. After running an AI model on Redwood, the model found ways to improve the chip itself, which he said suggests a self-reinforcing loop. "It's still very early, but we're very excited about the possibility of growing to larger models and getting AI to essentially recursively improve itself and build better and better hardware," Hussain said. Redwood can run AI models like Meta's Llama and Alibaba's Qwen, Architect said, though there's a caveat — it hasn't been manufactured yet. Instead, the design has been tested on reprogrammable hardware known as a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), and Architect said those tests suggest the finished product could be more efficient than Nvidia's Jetson Orin Nano , an AI supercomputer used in robotics. Hussain said the company plans to send Redwood to the Taiwanese chip manufacturer TSMC to be manufactured and hasn't decided when because its AI is still working to improve the design. Manufacturing is the real test, said Zheng, and it will ultimately reveal how fast, efficient, and reliable the chip is. Matthew Guthaus, a computer science and engineering professor at UC Santa Cruz, said that while AI is already good at many parts of chip design, "it can also make silly mistakes and needs close supervision and double-checking." These errors can cost millions if they aren't caught before manufacturing, Guthaus said. Hussain said that Architect's AI system checks its own work for mistakes rather than relying on humans to do so. Hussain said that AI could usher in a new era for the chip industry. While TSMC helped introduce a "fabless" era, allowing companies like Nvidia to design chips without owning factories, he says the next phase will be "designless" — putting custom chips within reach without the huge teams traditionally required to build them. items.title: Sam Altman knows people hate data centers
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has acknowledged the headwinds the AI industry is facing. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman knows people don't love AI right now. Altman told Time Magazine that "Clearly, people hate data centers—right now, at least." In the US, the AI industry is facing significant headwinds, especially in data center construction. Sam Altman doesn't need to see the polls . The OpenAI CEO knows how unpopular his industry has become. "Clearly, people hate data centers—right now, at least," Altman told Time as part of a series of interviews for a cover story published on Wednesday. "People are pretty negative on AI." Data centers in particular have become quite the pariah. Altman has previously spoken about the backlash against the industry, including local opposition to data center projects nationwide. "I understand emotionally why people don't want data centers in their backyard in the same way that I don't really want a nuclear power plant next to my house, even though I know it's a super safe thing," Altman said during an interview last month. In March, Altman was blunt in his assessment at a BlackRock event. "AI is not very popular in the US right now," Altman said during BlackRock's US Infrastructure Summit in Washington, D.C. In April, an attacker threw a Molotov cocktail at Altman's San Francisco mansion and later threatened to burn down OpenAI before being taken into custody. "A lot of the criticism of our industry comes from sincere concern about the incredibly high stakes of this technology," Altman wrote in a post on his personal blog after the attack. He added that "overall, I believe technological progress can make the future unbelievably good, for your family and mine. " Some companies, including OpenAI, have taken steps to address some of the biggest flashpoints in the data center debate, including water usage and power consumption. OpenAI has also announced community benefits, including Codex credits for eligible students in Ohio, Georgia, and Michigan, three places where it's building data centers. The backlash has only continued to grow In the last month, governors in Pennsylvania and Texas, both of whom are running for reelection in November, sought to curtail future data center development in their states after previously extolling the benefits of such projects. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, who once said his state was the "epicenter of AI development," said the industry had only itself to blame . "They pop up in places that nobody ever heard of before, until they started the construction," Abbott said on Sunday during an interview on ABC's "This Week". "And so, they had not been working in collaboration with the state, they'd not been in collaboration with local governments, and so they basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them and that's why they got the backlash they deserve." To top it all off, Super Bowl champion Jason Kelce starred in a cheeky ad for his and his brother Travis' beer company, Garage Beer, and canned water brand Liquid Death, where he suggested that people send their pee to data centers — adding a whole new dimension to the phrase "pissed off." Investor Chamath Palihapitiya, co-host of the "All-In Podcast," compared the situation to a "powder keg. " He said, "The safer bet may be that the pushback and resistance grow." "Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy," Palihapitiya wrote in a post on X last week. And even President Donald Trump , who has fashioned himself as a champion of the industry and argued that strict regulations could cost the US in the AI race, recently suggested data centers might benefit from a better message. "I would say that maybe it could use a little public relations help," Trump told reporters at the White House. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Alcohol became a flashpoint in the US-Canada trade war. Now both sides say they're losing.
items.summary: Alcohol makers in the US and Canada say they're hurting as a result of the trade war. John Fedele/Getty Images The US-Canada trade war escalated on Saturday with new 50% tariffs on Canadian alcohol. American booze was pulled from Canadian shelves last year and remains restricted in most of Canada. Alcohol makers in the US and Canada say both industries are hurting. What started as an eye-catching retaliation tactic to tariffs has become a sticking point in the US-Canada trade war — and neither side is standing down. The booze battle began last year after President Donald Trump imposed broad 25% tariffs on Canadian goods. Canada responded with its own 25% retaliatory tariffs targeting alcohol, among other products. The country's provinces went further, pulling American alcohol from shelves and halting new purchases or distribution. A year and a half later, American alcohol remains shut out of much of Canada. The boycott was so effective that Trump cited it as a driving force for his latest tariffs, including a 50% tariff on alcohol from Canada that took effect on Saturday after talks between the two countries broke down. While there's been plenty of finger-pointing about who started what, alcohol industries on both sides of the border say they're losing. "Our industry is really just an unfortunate victim," Chris Swonger, CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, said. "It's been devastating for the US industry over the last year and a half, and it's going to be significantly devastating for the Canadian spirits industry, but it'll trickle down and have an effect all the way from bartenders to our distributor partners to retailers to the American hospitality economy." Alcohol represents just a tiny sliver of the hundreds of billions of dollars in goods traded between the US and Canada, but the impact of the trade war on the industry has been especially severe and visible, in part due to the outright bans as well as the direct impact on beloved alcohol brands. For alcohol makers, the industry is also an unusual target for a trade war that's partially aimed at shifting manufacturing back to the US. Unlike other goods, alcohol is often prized specifically because of its country of origin. You can't make Canadian whisky in the US. "An American consumer may love Canadian whisky, and someone else may love tequila," Swonger said. The US and Canadian industries are calling for an end to the alcohol bans and tariffs Canadian provinces, which control alcohol imports, enacted bans on American alcohol around March 2025, the same month Canada levied its retaliatory tariffs. While those tariffs were lifted in September 2025, most of the province-level bans remained in place. Some provinces started allowing existing American stock to be sold, but continued to ban new imports. Eight out of 10 provinces still have some restrictions in place, with Alberta and Saskatchewan as the exceptions. The bans turned out to be one of the more headline-grabbing results of the trade war. They were also effective at inflicting economic pain: Imports of US alcohol to Canada fell by 81%, from about $718 million to $137 million, from March 2025 through February 2026, compared with the preceding year, according to the White House. In comparison, total US exports to Canada fell 4.8% in 2025. American alcohol makers felt they were being unfairly targeted. Lawson Whiting, CEO of Brown-Forman, the parent company of Jack Daniel's , said last year the bans were a "disproportionate" response to the tariffs. On an earnings call in June, the company said its organic sales in Canada fell nearly 60% in its 2026 fiscal year, as its products remained off shelves in most Canadian provinces. Canadian provinces banned American alcohol in early 2025. Most of those restrictions are still in place. VCG/VCG via Getty Images Now, Canadian makers, which are far more dependent on the US market than their American counterparts are on the Canadian market, face Trump's new 50% tariffs, which he said were a direct response to "Canadian discrimination" against American-made booze. The tariffs impact spirits, wine, and beer, with the most popular Canadian booze export to the US being Canadian whisky . Popular brands like Crown Royal, Canadian Club, and Fireball — the latter of which is made in America with imported Canadian whisky — could be affected. "Both the Canadian and American spirits industries have felt significant impacts of this broader trade dispute," Cal Bricker, President and CEO of Spirits Canada, said in a statement in July. Canadian spirit makers rely more heavily on exports to the US than American makers do on exports to Canada. Before the bans, Canada accounted for about 10% of US spirits exports. But 93% of all of Canada's spirits exports by value went to the US, according to Spirits Canada. Of all the spirits produced in Canada, nearly 50% are tied to US demand, the group says. The bans on American alcohol didn't necessarily translate to an increase in sales for Canadian makers, either. Following the bans, overall spirits sales in Canada fell about 4.4% by volume, while sales volumes of Canadian-made spirits were essentially flat, according to Spirits Canada. The alcohol bans were a key part of the failed negotiations The provincial bans became a major talking point last week as Canadian and US officials sought to make a deal to avoid new tariffs. Swonger said the alcohol industry feels it has unfairly become a "leverage point in broader trade negotiations." He said that while distillers appreciated Trump's efforts to prioritize the US alcohol industry going into negotiations, they also wanted to avoid the new 50% tariffs and get the bans lifted instead. Prime Minister Mark Carney asked Canadian provinces to return US alcohol to their shelves last week as the countries closed in on a deal. Officials in two provinces, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, signaled they were ready to lift bans on American alcohol if a broader deal was reached. Newfoundland said Thursday it would resume ordering American products, but changed course days later after the trade talks failed. Canadian makers have also been telling the Canadian provincial governments that the policy intended to punish America is endangering them as well. "While intended as a response to broader trade tensions, those measures have now become the stated basis for direct US retaliation against Canadian spirits exports," Spirits Canada said in July, encouraging the federal and provincial governments to work together to avoid US retaliation. Now, trade associations in Canada and the US are pushing for the same goal: end the mini trade war over alcohol. "We like to compete by sip and taste," Swonger said. "Not by trade barriers." "While intended as a response to broader trade tensions, those measures have now become the stated basis for direct US retaliation against Canadian spirits exports," Spirits Canada said in July, encouraging the federal and provincial governments to work together to avoid US retaliation.

Now, trade associations in Canada and the US are pushing for the same goal: end the mini trade war over alcohol.

"We like to compete by sip and taste," Swonger said. "Not by trade barriers."

items.title: What smart people are saying about Meta's settlement
items.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg arrives to the Los Angeles Superior Court at United States Court House on February 18, 2026. Meta agreed to put greater restrictions on teen users on Wednesday. Jill Connelly/Getty Images Meta settled a teen social media addiction lawsuit with states for about $18 billion. Some experts called the deal shrewd, saying Meta avoided potentially massive damages. Critics say the deal is too weak and its teen protections could prove difficult to enforce. Attorneys and analysts are divided on whether Meta made the right move. The social media giant on Wednesday settled with a group of states that sued the company in 2023 and alleged that it had designed its social media platforms to be addictive to teenagers. Included in the settlement are a slew of restrictions for teen users of Instagram and Facebook. If the federal judge overseeing the case approves the settlement, teen users will be limited to two hours of scrolling per day, will be unable to scroll at night, and won't get notifications during the school day. Also in the settlement is around $18 billion for 47 states, the District of Columbia, and several American territories, to be paid out by Meta in installments over the next decade. Around $5 billion of that sum is contingent upon YouTube and TikTok also coughing up billions and instituting similar controls for teen users. Meta and the attorneys general struck the deal less than two weeks after the trial began. Here's what smart people are saying about Meta's landmark social media settlement. Ari Cohn, First Amendment lawyer Cohn, a First Amendment lawyer in Chicago, called the settlement a "shrewd business move, but awful for free speech." Cohn said that by calling on YouTube and TikTok to institute similar restrictions, Meta is "attempting regulatory capture" by setting a standard it hopes rival social media giants will follow. Uttara Ananthakrishnan, associate professor at the University of Washington Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington, told Business Insider that she wouldn't be surprised if YouTube and TikTok announce similar restrictions in the coming days. Ananthakrishnan, who has authored several research papers about the addictive qualities of TikTok, said that while she welcomed the restrictions announced Wednesday, she doubts they'll live up to expectations. "Meta doesn't have a great reputation of enforcing its own policies," she said. Ananthakrishnan pointed to a teen social media ban in Australia , which has largely failed to keep young users off the platforms, as a reason why it's difficult for companies to verify checks. "Enforcement is going to be really difficult," she said. "A motivated, 16-year-old and 18-year-old will just adopt a VPN, log in from their parents' accounts or whatever." Jonathan Turley, professor at George Washington University Law School Jonathan Turley, a professor at George Washington University Law School, said Meta's monetary payout was a big lowball. "The $16 billion is a bit like monopoly money," Turley wrote on X. "Meta succeeded in tying off the potential for massive damages while making changes that was already moving to incorporate in its platform." Turley added that although the settlement will lead to new protections for children on social media, they will ultimately not last. "The technology is too popular and too accessible to create a true firewall," Turley wrote. "The burden will remain with parents." Jason Kint, CEO of Digital Content Next Jason Kint, who leads Digital Content Next, a trade organization that represents digital media companies, said the case impacts an entire generation of children. "Wow. $16 BILLION means Meta/Facebook/Instagram is now approaching $25 BILLION they've on settlements related to consumer protection abuses," he wrote on X on Wednesday. Gary Marcus, tech researcher and writer Marcus, a tech researcher, wrote on X that he hopes other social media platforms will follow suit with guardrails. "I hope that X, TikTok, and YouTube will match these social media restrictions for teens, including 'Productive Pauses,' 'Nighttime blocks,' limited school-time access for children, tighter content controls, stronger and more straightforward parental controls, and limits on things like beauty filters and visible likes," he wrote on Wednesday. He added, "Adults (me included!) would be wise to opt-in for a lot of the same." Read the original article on Business Insider

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg arrives to the Los Angeles Superior Court at United States Court House on February 18, 2026. Meta agreed to put greater restrictions on teen users on Wednesday.

Jill Connelly/Getty Images

  • Meta settled a teen social media addiction lawsuit with states for about $18 billion.
  • Some experts called the deal shrewd, saying Meta avoided potentially massive damages.
  • Critics say the deal is too weak and its teen protections could prove difficult to enforce.

Attorneys and analysts are divided on whether Meta made the right move.

The social media giant on Wednesday settled with a group of states that sued the company in 2023 and alleged that it had designed its social media platforms to be addictive to teenagers.

Included in the settlement are a slew of restrictions for teen users of Instagram and Facebook. If the federal judge overseeing the case approves the settlement, teen users will be limited to two hours of scrolling per day, will be unable to scroll at night, and won't get notifications during the school day.

Also in the settlement is around $18 billion for 47 states, the District of Columbia, and several American territories, to be paid out by Meta in installments over the next decade. Around $5 billion of that sum is contingent upon YouTube and TikTok also coughing up billions and instituting similar controls for teen users.

Meta and the attorneys general struck the deal less than two weeks after the trial began.

Here's what smart people are saying about Meta's landmark social media settlement.

Ari Cohn, First Amendment lawyer

Cohn, a First Amendment lawyer in Chicago, called the settlement a "shrewd business move, but awful for free speech."

Cohn said that by calling on YouTube and TikTok to institute similar restrictions, Meta is "attempting regulatory capture" by setting a standard it hopes rival social media giants will follow.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, associate professor at the University of Washington

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington, told Business Insider that she wouldn't be surprised if YouTube and TikTok announce similar restrictions in the coming days.

Ananthakrishnan, who has authored several research papers about the addictive qualities of TikTok, said that while she welcomed the restrictions announced Wednesday, she doubts they'll live up to expectations.

"Meta doesn't have a great reputation of enforcing its own policies," she said.

Ananthakrishnan pointed to a teen social media ban in Australia, which has largely failed to keep young users off the platforms, as a reason why it's difficult for companies to verify checks.

"Enforcement is going to be really difficult," she said. "A motivated, 16-year-old and 18-year-old will just adopt a VPN, log in from their parents' accounts or whatever."

Jonathan Turley, professor at George Washington University Law School

Jonathan Turley, a professor at George Washington University Law School, said Meta's monetary payout was a big lowball.

"The $16 billion is a bit like monopoly money," Turley wrote on X. "Meta succeeded in tying off the potential for massive damages while making changes that was already moving to incorporate in its platform."

Turley added that although the settlement will lead to new protections for children on social media, they will ultimately not last.

"The technology is too popular and too accessible to create a true firewall," Turley wrote. "The burden will remain with parents."

Jason Kint, CEO of Digital Content Next

Jason Kint, who leads Digital Content Next, a trade organization that represents digital media companies, said the case impacts an entire generation of children.

"Wow. $16 BILLION means Meta/Facebook/Instagram is now approaching $25 BILLION they've on settlements related to consumer protection abuses," he wrote on X on Wednesday.

Gary Marcus, tech researcher and writer

Marcus, a tech researcher, wrote on X that he hopes other social media platforms will follow suit with guardrails.

"I hope that X, TikTok, and YouTube will match these social media restrictions for teens, including 'Productive Pauses,' 'Nighttime blocks,' limited school-time access for children, tighter content controls, stronger and more straightforward parental controls, and limits on things like beauty filters and visible likes," he wrote on Wednesday.

He added, "Adults (me included!) would be wise to opt-in for a lot of the same."

items.title: Tennis star Taylor Fritz says playing video games helps keep his brain 'working well' on the court
items.summary: Tennis star Taylor Fritz said playing "League of Legends" helps him decompress. Mike Lawrence/USTA via Getty Images Tennis star Taylor Fritz said playing video games helps him perform better on the court. He enjoys playing "League of Legends," and said the game helps him sharpen his focus. He had also been playing the game in the lead-up to his 2023 Atlanta Open win, he said. Taylor Fritz , 28, said playing " League of Legends " is as much a part of his tennis routine as sleep and recovery. Speaking to GQ in an interview published on Wednesday, the tennis star said playing video games helps him decompress. "When you're training and traveling, you don't always have the energy — nor even should you be going out and doing stuff. You need that time to do something that's not as active," Fritz said. Fritz said he had also seen studies suggesting that the video game he plays, "League of Legends," can improve focus. Developed by Riot Games, the game pits two teams of five against each other, with the goal of destroying the enemy's base. He added that he's experienced those effects himself. "I've definitely noticed crossover: When I feel like my brain's working well when I'm playing the game, my brain's working well when I'm on the court," Fritz said. In the lead-up to his 2023 Atlanta Open win, Fritz said he had been having a good week playing "League of Legends" too, and felt mentally sharp heading into the tournament. "It's like playing chess with pieces that are almost moving without your control. I could feel that my mind was just working really well, and then I could feel that whole week on the court as well," Fritz said. "It was very obvious to me that my decision-making and focus were elevated that week," he continued. Gaming is one part of Fritz's off-court routine. To stay in top shape, he said he aims to eat 200 grams of protein a day and has a go-to Chipotle order that helps him hit that target without going overboard on calories. "It was a lighter portion of rice, no beans, double chicken, the fajita veggies, and then I would go really light sour cream and cheese," Fritz said, adding that he gets hot salsa on the side. With the demanding travel and match schedule on tour, Fritz said he also has to manage his sleep carefully. He adjusts his bedtime depending on when he is due to play a match. If he knows he'll be playing a match at night, he'll start shifting his body clock a few days beforehand by going to sleep as late as 1 a.m. and waking around late morning or noon. "And I'm just starting to get on this weird sleep cycle to where I will feel very awake and ready to play my match if I'm playing at eight," he said. Fritz has previously spoken about the habits that help him stay healthy and focused on tour. He told Business Insider in 2022 that Chipotle is a regular part of his diet during tournament season. "I think a lot of people don't understand how good it is as a post-workout meal. It's got everything," he said. In 2023, Fritz told Business Insider that he needs to have a high-protein breakfast . "I usually don't eat a lot for breakfast, but I always have protein of some kind. I never start my day without it," Fritz said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Motion lands $2M to expand humanoid robot deployments across Europe
items.summary:
Brussels-based
robotics company Motion has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding to expand its
Humanoids-as-a-Service (HaaS) platform and move its existing industrial pilots
into commercial deployment. The round was led by Extantia Capital , with
participation from Norrsken Evolve . Founded
in 2026, Motion provides humanoid robots to industrial, warehouse and logistics
companies through a subscription-based model designed to reduce the upfront
cost and operational complexity associated with adopting the technology. Rather
than requiring customers to purchase and deploy robots themselves, Motion
charges a monthly fee covering the deployment process, including data
collection, robot selection, task training, IT integration, fleet management,
financing, insurance, compliance and maintenance. Motion
is currently running five pilots with industrial, warehouse and logistics
companies in Belgium. Its humanoid robots are being trained for tasks including
loading goods into crates, packing containers into boxes and placing components
on conveyor belts, working alongside existing employees. The
company is positioning its technology as one way to address labour shortages
across European manufacturing, where businesses are increasingly struggling to
fill operational roles. However, Motion says the adoption of humanoid robots
remains limited by financing, integration, regulatory and operational
requirements associated with deploying and managing robotic fleets. Europe
has a robot adoption problem. Adoption fails on financing, risk and compliance
long before it fails on technology. So we take everything that stands between a
factory and its first humanoid and turn it into one predictable monthly fee.
Hiring a robot should be as easy as hiring a person, said Alexander Stevens ,
founder and CEO of Motion. The
company's hardware-agnostic model is designed to allow customers to use robots
suited to specific applications without committing to a single manufacturer.
Motion also operates a European software layer through which deployment
experience can be applied across its network while individual customers retain
control of their data. Alongside
its direct deployments, Motion is launching a partner programme for system
integrators and automation specialists, enabling them to deploy humanoid robots
for their own customers using Motion's platform. The new
funding will be used to move Motion's five existing pilots into full
production, expand its team and increase its robot fleet. The company will
initially focus on growing across the Benelux region.
items.summary_html:
Brussels-based robotics company Motion has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding to expand its Humanoids-as-a-Service (HaaS) platform and move its existing industrial pilots into commercial deployment. The round was led by Extantia Capital, with participation from Norrsken Evolve.

Founded in 2026, Motion provides humanoid robots to industrial, warehouse and logistics companies through a subscription-based model designed to reduce the upfront cost and operational complexity associated with adopting the technology.

Rather than requiring customers to purchase and deploy robots themselves, Motion charges a monthly fee covering the deployment process, including data collection, robot selection, task training, IT integration, fleet management, financing, insurance, compliance and maintenance.

Motion is currently running five pilots with industrial, warehouse and logistics companies in Belgium. Its humanoid robots are being trained for tasks including loading goods into crates, packing containers into boxes and placing components on conveyor belts, working alongside existing employees.

The company is positioning its technology as one way to address labour shortages across European manufacturing, where businesses are increasingly struggling to fill operational roles. However, Motion says the adoption of humanoid robots remains limited by financing, integration, regulatory and operational requirements associated with deploying and managing robotic fleets.

Europe has a robot adoption problem. Adoption fails on financing, risk and compliance long before it fails on technology. So we take everything that stands between a factory and its first humanoid and turn it into one predictable monthly fee. Hiring a robot should be as easy as hiring a person,

said Alexander Stevens, founder and CEO of Motion.

The company's hardware-agnostic model is designed to allow customers to use robots suited to specific applications without committing to a single manufacturer. Motion also operates a European software layer through which deployment experience can be applied across its network while individual customers retain control of their data.

Alongside its direct deployments, Motion is launching a partner programme for system integrators and automation specialists, enabling them to deploy humanoid robots for their own customers using Motion's platform.

The new funding will be used to move Motion's five existing pilots into full production, expand its team and increase its robot fleet. The company will initially focus on growing across the Benelux region.

items.title: I Gave Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 the Exact Same Build Task. The Results Surprised Me.
items.summary: Two frontier models, one identical spec, zero hand holding. Here’s what actually happened when I stopped reading benchmark charts and just watched them work. Side-by-side spec comparison: Claude Fable 5 versus GPT-5.6 Sol. I’ve read enough model comparison posts to know how most of them go. Someone pulls two benchmark tables, screenshots them side by side, and calls it a review. I wanted something less theoretical. So I picked one real build task, gave the exact same prompt to Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, and just watched what each one actually did no cherry picking, no re rolling until I got a good answer. What I found lines up with the numbers in a way I didn’t expect, but it also exposed a few things no spec sheet tells you. The Setup Both of these are genuinely frontier-tier models, released within a month of each other. Claude Fable 5 came out June 9, 2026, and Anthropic calls it the most capable model it has ever shipped. GPT-5.6 Sol followed on July 9, 2026, as the top tier of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family, sitting above the mid-tier Terra and lighter Luna variants. On paper they’re close cousins: both sit around a 1 million-token context window, both max out near 128,000 output tokens, both are built for serious agentic work. The real difference shows up in the receipt. Fable 5 runs $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output. Sol runs about half that roughly $5 and $30 though its pricing steps up once you cross 272,000 input tokens in a single request, which quietly erases some of that headline discount on longer jobs. Testing agentic planning and resilience on a real-world full-stack task. I gave both models the same task: build a small full-stack app a task tracker with user authentication, a REST API, a Postgres schema, and a React frontend from a single written spec, with no follow-up clarifying questions allowed. I wanted to see planning, execution, and how each one handled the inevitable point where something breaks. Round One: How They Opened This is where the personalities showed up immediately. Sol went straight into motion. It broke the spec into a task list, spun up the project scaffolding, and started writing files within seconds of me hitting enter. It felt like watching someone who’d done this exact task a hundred times and didn’t need to think out loud about it. Fable 5 took longer to get moving. It spent noticeably more time reasoning through the schema design and the auth flow before touching a single file weighing where sessions should live, how to structure the API routes, what edge cases the spec was quietly implying. It felt less like a fast typist and more like an engineer sketching the architecture on a whiteboard before opening the editor. Neither approach is “wrong,” but if you’re the kind of developer who wants to see progress immediately, Sol wins that first impression easily. Round Two: The Actual Build Once both were rolling, the gap in style became a gap in outcome . Sol’s code came out clean and idiomatic, and it moved through the terminal like it owned the place running commands, checking outputs, correcting course, all with very little friction. That tracks with what OpenAI has published: Sol posts a strong 88.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, the benchmark that specifically measures autonomous command-line work, and even climbs to 91.9% in its subagent-orchestration “Ultra” mode. Fable 5’s build was slower to arrive but noticeably more resilient once it did. It caught two edge cases in my spec that Sol didn’t a race condition in the auth token refresh logic, and a missing cascade rule in the database schema that would have silently orphaned records. Nobody told either model to look for those. Fable 5 just didn’t move on until the design held up under its own questioning. That difference wasn’t a fluke on my one test. It matches the widest, most consistently reported gap between these two models: SWE bench Pro, which measures whether a model can resolve real GitHub issues end-to-end across a codebase, not just drive a terminal. Fable 5 scores around 80% there. Sol hasn’t published a comparable number, and independent aggregators note the models simply don’t have full overlapping coverage on this specific benchmark yet. How GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5 approach full-stack development across three distinct rounds. Round Three: Where It Actually Broke I deliberately introduced a bug after the first build a subtly wrong foreign key reference and asked both models to fix it without telling them where the problem was. Sol found it fast, in under a minute of tool calls, but its first patch only addressed the symptom (a failing query) rather than the schema-level cause. A second nudge got it to the real fix. Fable 5 took longer to respond, but traced the error back through the schema on its own reasoning pass and fixed the actual source in one attempt. This is consistent with the broader pattern reviewers keep landing on: terminal and tool-driven debugging favors Sol on speed, while root-cause reasoning across a codebase favors Fable 5. Different tests are measuring different muscles, and both models are strong just not at the same thing. The Numbers Side by Side Here’s how the two stack up on the benchmarks that actually matter for this kind of work, pulled from official release material and independent trackers as of late July 2026: For scale on what “12 hours of autonomy” actually looks like in production: Anthropic has cited a case where Stripe used Fable 5 to complete a 50-million-line Ruby migration in a single day the kind of task that isn’t really a fair comparison for either model on a laptop, but it tells you what the top end of “long-running” means for Fable 5 specifically. What the Price Difference Actually Buys You I tracked token spend across both runs. Sol finished the base build using meaningfully fewer output tokens OpenAI has cited roughly a 54% improvement in token efficiency for this generation and at roughly half Fable 5’s per-token price, the total cost gap for my task was significant, not marginal. Fable 5’s bill was higher on this specific job, but the two defect fixes it caught unprompted are exactly the kind of thing that costs real engineering hours to find in code review or, worse, in production. If you’re pricing this by “cost per correct outcome” rather than “cost per token,” the math gets a lot closer than the sticker price suggests. So Which One Actually Won? Honestly neither, cleanly. That’s the part that surprised me, because I expected the benchmark gap to translate into an obvious winner, and it didn’t. Sol is the better choice when: You want fast iteration and don’t mind a second pass on fixes Your work leans heavily on terminal and tool use automation Token cost matters more than squeezing out the last percentage of correctness Fable 5 is the better choice when: You’re touching a large, unfamiliar, or high-stakes codebase The cost of a missed edge case is higher than the cost of extra tokens You’re running long, multi hour autonomous jobs and need it to hold together the whole way through Match Sol to your fast terminal tasks and save Fable 5 for your complex, root-cause architecture builds. If your instinct is to pick one and standardize on it forever, I’d push back on that instinct. The gap between these two isn’t about which one is smarter it’s about which failure mode you’d rather live with: Sol moving fast and needing a second look, or Fable 5 moving deliberately and costing you more per token to get there. What I got instead was a much more useful answer: two models that are excellent at genuinely different jobs, priced accordingly, and honest in their own published numbers about where they don’t lead. If there’s one thing I’d tell another developer before they run this same test themselves: don’t grade the result by which one “felt” smarter in the first two minutes. Grade it by what’s still standing after you’ve tried to break it. The future of AI-driven coding isn’t about finding one model to rule them all. Sol gives you rapid execution and terminal fluency at half the cost, while Fable 5 delivers deep architectural resilience when failure isn’t an option. The smartest engineering workflow uses both — matching the tool to the critical nature of the task. And if this saved you the afternoon I spent building it twice, a clap goes a long way. I Gave Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 the Exact Same Build Task.
